Employee Attrition Prediction & Workforce Risk Analysis¶

Domain: Human Resources / People Analytics
End consumer: HR Manager / People Analytics Manager
ML type: Supervised learning — binary classification
Target: Attrition (Yes / No)
Models: Logistic Regression · Random Forest · XGBoost
Explainability: SHAP
Dataset: IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition & Performance (WA_Fn-UseC_-HR-Employee-Attrition.csv, 1,470 employees × 35 columns)

Workflow¶

Business Understanding → Data Loading → Data Quality → Cleaning → 10 KPIs → 10 Univariate → 10 Bivariate → 10 Multivariate → Feature Engineering → Preprocessing → Logistic Regression → Random Forest → XGBoost → Model Evaluation → Threshold Analysis → SHAP → Business Insights → HR Recommendations → Limitations → Conclusion

Integrity note. Every number quoted in the markdown of this notebook was produced by the code cells directly above or below it, run against the uploaded dataset. Associations described here are observational; neither correlations nor SHAP values establish that a factor causes attrition.

Stage 1 — Project Introduction¶

Business problem¶

Employee attrition increases recruitment and onboarding costs, disrupts teams, drains institutional knowledge and reduces productivity while replacements ramp up. HR teams usually learn about a resignation only when it happens. If the organisation can (a) understand which employee groups show elevated attrition and (b) estimate each employee's probability of leaving, it can direct supportive, voluntary retention conversations and structural fixes where they are most needed.

End consumer¶

An HR Manager / People Analytics Manager who needs plain-language answers, defensible numbers and a clear sense of what the model can and cannot be trusted to do.

Objectives¶

# Question the HR Manager is asking Where it is answered
1 What proportion of employees leave? KPIs, Univariate U1
2 Which employee groups have higher observed attrition? Bivariate & Multivariate
3 What characteristics are associated with attrition? EDA, SHAP
4 How accurately can attrition be predicted? Model evaluation
5 Which model performs best on appropriate metrics? Model comparison
6 Which features contribute most to model predictions? SHAP
7 What evidence-based retention actions could HR investigate? Insights & Recommendations

Target variable¶

Attrition — Yes if the employee left, No otherwise. Encoded as 1 = Yes (left), 0 = No (stayed); the positive class is the event HR wants to anticipate.

Expected business value¶

  • A quantified baseline of workforce attrition and the groups where it concentrates.
  • A validated probability-of-leaving model with an explicit, business-chosen decision threshold.
  • Transparent explanations of what drives the model's risk scores (SHAP), suitable for HR stakeholders.
  • A prioritised list of retention areas to investigate — not a list of people to penalise.

Ethical guardrails¶

Risk scores are intended to prompt supportive actions (career conversations, workload review, compensation benchmarking). They must never be used for punitive decisions such as exclusion from promotion, training or projects. Protected or sensitive attributes (e.g. Gender, MaritalStatus, Age) are retained for analysis transparency, but any operational use should be reviewed by HR, Legal and the Data Protection function.

Stage 2 — Environment Setup¶

All libraries are imported once here. A single global seed (SEED = 42) is used for NumPy, Python's random, every train/test split, cross-validation fold and model, so the notebook reproduces identical results on re-run.

Reusable helper functions¶

Small helpers keep the 40 analyses consistent: every group comparison reports headcount, leavers and attrition rate, and every heatmap shows the sample size of each cell so that small subgroups are visibly flagged rather than over-interpreted.

In [2]:
def save_fig(fig, name):
    # Save a figure to reports/figures for reuse in the README / report.
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / f"{name}.png", bbox_inches="tight")

def rate_table(data, by, target="AttritionFlag"):
    # Headcount, leavers and attrition rate (%) for one or more grouping columns.
    t = (data.groupby(by, observed=True)[target]
             .agg(Employees="count", Leavers="sum", Rate="mean"))
    t["AttritionRate_%"] = (t.pop("Rate") * 100).round(1)
    return t

def rate_bar(ax, table, title, overall=None, color=ACCENT, rotate=0):
    # Bar chart of attrition rate with headcount labels and an optional company-average line.
    x = [str(i) for i in table.index]
    bars = ax.bar(x, table["AttritionRate_%"], color=color, edgecolor="white")
    for b, (r, n) in zip(bars, zip(table["AttritionRate_%"], table["Employees"])):
        ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, b.get_height() + 0.6, f"{r:.1f}%\n(n={n})",
                ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8)
    if overall is not None:
        ax.axhline(overall, ls="--", color="grey", lw=1, label=f"Company avg {overall:.1f}%")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylabel("Attrition rate (%)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(table["AttritionRate_%"].max() * 1.30, 5))
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=rotate)

def rate_heatmap(ax, data, row, col, title, min_n=20, target="AttritionFlag"):
    # Heatmap of attrition rate for row x col; cells with n < min_n are hatched and marked '*'.
    rate = data.pivot_table(index=row, columns=col, values=target, aggfunc="mean", observed=True) * 100
    n = data.pivot_table(index=row, columns=col, values=target, aggfunc="count", observed=True)
    im = ax.imshow(rate.values, cmap="Reds", vmin=0, vmax=max(50, np.nanmax(rate.values)), aspect="auto")
    for i in range(rate.shape[0]):
        for j in range(rate.shape[1]):
            r, c = rate.values[i, j], n.values[i, j]
            if np.isnan(r):
                ax.text(j, i, "—", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color="grey")
                continue
            small = c < min_n
            if small:   # hatch cells too small to interpret
                ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j - 0.5, i - 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, hatch="///",
                                           edgecolor="grey", lw=0, alpha=0.6))
            ax.text(j, i, f"{r:.0f}%{'*' if small else ''}\nn={int(c)}", ha="center", va="center",
                    fontsize=8, color=("white" if (r > 30 and not small) else "black"),
                    fontweight=("normal" if small else "bold"),
                    bbox=(dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.75) if small else None))
    ax.set_xticks(range(rate.shape[1])); ax.set_xticklabels([str(c) for c in rate.columns])
    ax.set_yticks(range(rate.shape[0])); ax.set_yticklabels([str(r) for r in rate.index])
    ax.set_xlabel(col); ax.set_ylabel(row); ax.set_title(title)
    ax.grid(False)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.035, label="Attrition rate (%)")
    return rate.round(1), n

def cramers_v(x, y):
    # Cramer's V effect size + chi-square p-value for two categorical variables.
    ct = pd.crosstab(x, y)
    chi2, p, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
    v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (ct.values.sum() * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
    return v, p

Finding. Data types are appropriate: numeric fields are integers and categorical fields are text. All ordinal codes fall inside their documented ranges (satisfaction/involvement 1–4, education 1–5, job level 1–5, stock option level 0–3). Note that PerformanceRating only takes the values 3 and 4 — the lower ratings (1–2) never occur, so this field has very little spread. All logical consistency checks return zero violations (e.g. nobody has more years in their current role than at the company, and every employee started work aged 18 or older). No invalid values were found.

Finding. Three columns are constant: EmployeeCount (always 1), Over18 (always "Y") and StandardHours (always 80). A constant carries zero information for distinguishing leavers from stayers. EmployeeNumber is a unique identifier; any pattern a model learned from it would be an artefact of how IDs were assigned, not a workforce characteristic. These four columns are candidates for removal in Stage 5.

4.4 Potential outliers (IQR rule)¶

In [11]:
cont_cols = ["Age", "DailyRate", "DistanceFromHome", "HourlyRate", "MonthlyIncome", "MonthlyRate",
             "NumCompaniesWorked", "PercentSalaryHike", "TotalWorkingYears", "TrainingTimesLastYear",
             "YearsAtCompany", "YearsInCurrentRole", "YearsSinceLastPromotion", "YearsWithCurrManager"]
rows = []
for c in cont_cols:
    q1, q3 = df_raw[c].quantile([0.25, 0.75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    n_out = ((df_raw[c] < lo) | (df_raw[c] > hi)).sum()
    rows.append([c, df_raw[c].min(), df_raw[c].max(), round(df_raw[c].skew(), 2), n_out,
                 round(100 * n_out / len(df_raw), 1)])
outliers = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Feature", "Min", "Max", "Skew", "IQR_outliers", "Outlier_%"])
display(outliers.sort_values("IQR_outliers", ascending=False).set_index("Feature"))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.5))
for ax, c in zip(axes, ["MonthlyIncome", "YearsAtCompany", "TotalWorkingYears", "YearsSinceLastPromotion"]):
    ax.boxplot(df_raw[c], vert=True, widths=0.5, patch_artist=True, boxprops=dict(facecolor="#cfe0f3"))
    ax.set_title(c); ax.set_xticks([])
fig.suptitle("Features with the most IQR outliers", fontweight="bold"); plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "dq_outliers"); plt.show()

Finding. MonthlyIncome (114 IQR outliers), YearsSinceLastPromotion (107), YearsAtCompany (104) and TotalWorkingYears (63) are right-skewed. These "outliers" are plausible real values — senior, long-tenured, highly paid employees (maximum income 19,999; maximum tenure 40 years) — not data-entry errors. Removing or capping them would delete exactly the senior population HR needs to understand. Decision: retain them. Tree models are insensitive to monotone scale; for Logistic Regression we standardise features, and we note skew as a limitation rather than distorting the data.

4.5 Class imbalance¶

In [12]:
counts = df_raw["Attrition"].value_counts()
ratio = counts["No"] / counts["Yes"]
print(f"Stayed (No): {counts['No']}  |  Left (Yes): {counts['Yes']}  |  imbalance ratio {ratio:.2f} : 1")
print(f"A naive model predicting 'No' for everyone would score {counts['No']/counts.sum():.1%} accuracy "
      f"while identifying 0% of leavers.")

Stayed (No): 1233  |  Left (Yes): 237  |  imbalance ratio 5.20 : 1
A naive model predicting 'No' for everyone would score 83.9% accuracy while identifying 0% of leavers.

Finding. Roughly 5.2 stayers for every leaver. A useless model that always predicts "stays" achieves 83.9 % accuracy — so accuracy is a misleading headline metric here. We will (a) stratify the train/test split, (b) use class-weighting or scale_pos_weight where it helps, (c) tune models on PR-AUC (average precision), which focuses on the minority class, and (d) choose the decision threshold explicitly.

4.6 Multicollinearity check¶

In [13]:
num_df = df_raw.drop(columns=["EmployeeCount", "StandardHours", "EmployeeNumber"]).select_dtypes("number")
corr = num_df.corr()
pairs = (corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), 1).astype(bool)).stack()
             .rename("r").reset_index().rename(columns={"level_0": "Feature A", "level_1": "Feature B"}))
pairs["|r|"] = pairs["r"].abs()
display(pairs.sort_values("|r|", ascending=False).head(8).set_index(["Feature A", "Feature B"]).round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 9))
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(corr))); ax.set_xticklabels(corr.columns, rotation=90, fontsize=7)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(corr))); ax.set_yticklabels(corr.columns, fontsize=7)
ax.grid(False); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.04); ax.set_title("Correlation matrix — numeric features")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "dq_correlation_matrix"); plt.show()
r |r|
Feature A Feature B
JobLevel MonthlyIncome 0.950 0.950
TotalWorkingYears 0.782 0.782
PercentSalaryHike PerformanceRating 0.774 0.774
MonthlyIncome TotalWorkingYears 0.773 0.773
YearsAtCompany YearsWithCurrManager 0.769 0.769
YearsInCurrentRole 0.759 0.759
YearsInCurrentRole YearsWithCurrManager 0.714 0.714
Age TotalWorkingYears 0.680 0.680

Finding. JobLevel and MonthlyIncome are almost interchangeable (r ≈ 0.95), and the tenure variables (YearsAtCompany, YearsInCurrentRole, YearsWithCurrManager) are strongly inter-correlated (r ≈ 0.71–0.77). PercentSalaryHike and PerformanceRating are also correlated (r ≈ 0.77). This does not hurt predictive accuracy much, but it means individual coefficients and SHAP values can be split between correlated partners, so we interpret feature groups ("pay/level", "tenure") rather than over-reading one variable. We use L2-regularised Logistic Regression, which is stable under correlated inputs. All features are kept.

4.7 Potential target leakage¶

Target leakage occurs when a predictor contains information that would only be known after (or because) the outcome happened.

Check Assessment
Columns derived from the exit event (exit-interview scores, termination date, notice period) None present.
Identifier (EmployeeNumber) Not causal leakage, but a spurious signal risk → removed.
Snapshot timing of tenure fields (YearsAtCompany, YearsInCurrentRole, YearsWithCurrManager) The dataset does not document when the snapshot was taken. For leavers these were likely recorded at exit. This is a residual risk: in production, scoring must use values as of the scoring date.
MonthlyRate, DailyRate, HourlyRate Not leakage; but they do not reconcile with MonthlyIncome, suggesting synthetic generation (see Limitations). Kept; the model will decide their usefulness.

Conclusion: no direct leakage columns. The tenure-timing caveat is documented in Limitations.

Stage 5 — Data Cleaning¶

Only justified changes are made:

Action Columns Justification
Drop EmployeeCount, Over18, StandardHours Constant (one unique value) — zero information.
Drop EmployeeNumber Unique identifier — no workforce meaning; risk of spurious learning. Kept separately for traceability of predictions.
Add AttritionFlag 1 = Yes, 0 = No — numeric target for rates and modelling.
Keep All other 30 predictors No missing/invalid values; outliers are genuine; correlated features retained (see 4.6).

Analysis-only band columns (e.g. age bands) are created inside a separate EDA frame so that they never enter the modelling feature set.

In [14]:
DROP_COLS = ["EmployeeCount", "Over18", "StandardHours", "EmployeeNumber"]
employee_ids = df_raw["EmployeeNumber"].copy()        # kept for traceability only
df = df_raw.drop(columns=DROP_COLS).copy()
df["AttritionFlag"] = (df["Attrition"] == "Yes").astype(int)
print(f"Cleaned shape: {df.shape}  (removed {len(DROP_COLS)} columns, added AttritionFlag)")

# EDA-only copy with readable bands (never used as model inputs)
eda = df.copy()
eda["AgeBand"] = pd.cut(eda.Age, [17, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 60],
                        labels=["18-25", "26-30", "31-35", "36-40", "41-50", "51-60"])
eda["IncomeQuartile"] = pd.qcut(eda.MonthlyIncome, 4, labels=["Q1 (lowest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 (highest)"])
eda["TenureBand"] = pd.cut(eda.YearsAtCompany, [-1, 1, 3, 5, 10, 40], labels=["0-1", "2-3", "4-5", "6-10", "11+"])
eda["DistanceBand"] = pd.cut(eda.DistanceFromHome, [0, 5, 10, 20, 29], labels=["1-5", "6-10", "11-20", "21-29"])
eda["CareerBand"] = pd.cut(eda.TotalWorkingYears, [-1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40], labels=["0-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-20", "21+"])
print(eda.groupby("IncomeQuartile", observed=True)["MonthlyIncome"].agg(["min", "max"]))
OVERALL_RATE = eda["AttritionFlag"].mean() * 100

Phase 1 — 10 HR KPIs¶

Each KPI follows Business Question → Technical Question → Calculation → Python Code → Actual Result → HR Interpretation. All ten are computed in one cell (so they share one definition of the data) and then interpreted individually.

KPI 1 — Total Employees¶

  • Business question: How large is the workforce covered by this analysis?
  • Technical question: What is the unit of analysis, and is each row one unique employee?
  • Calculation: len(df) — count of rows after confirming no duplicates and a unique EmployeeNumber.
  • Actual result: 1,470 employees.
  • HR interpretation: This is a mid-sized workforce snapshot. It is large enough for headline rates but small enough that some role × department sub-groups contain only a few dozen people, so subgroup findings need caution.
  • Technical answer: One row = one employee (verified in 4.1); the sample size bounds the precision of every rate we compute.

KPI 2 — Total Employees Who Left¶

  • Business question: How many people did we lose?
  • Technical question: How many positive-class examples does the model have to learn from?
  • Calculation: df.AttritionFlag.sum().
  • Actual result: 237 leavers.
  • HR interpretation: 237 vacancies represent significant recruitment, onboarding and lost-productivity cost.
  • Technical answer: Only 237 positive examples (≈ 190 in training after an 80/20 split) limits model complexity and makes cross-validation essential.

KPI 3 — Overall Attrition Rate¶

  • Business question: What proportion of our employees leave?
  • Technical question: What is the base rate (prior probability) of the positive class?
  • Calculation: leavers ÷ total × 100.
  • Actual result: 16.12 %.
  • HR interpretation: About one in six employees in the dataset left. This is the benchmark every group comparison below is measured against.
  • Technical answer: The base rate is also the PR-AUC of a random classifier (≈ 0.16), so any useful model must clearly exceed it.

KPI 4 — Average Employee Age¶

  • Business question: How mature is our workforce?
  • Technical question: What is the central tendency of Age, and is the mean representative?
  • Calculation: df.Age.mean().
  • Actual result: 36.92 years (median 36 — see U2).
  • HR interpretation: A mid-career workforce. Later analysis shows attrition is concentrated in the youngest segment, so the average hides an important tail.
  • Technical answer: Age is only mildly skewed, so the mean is a fair summary.

KPI 5 — Average Monthly Income¶

  • Business question: What is our typical pay level?
  • Technical question: Is the mean a good summary of a skewed income distribution?
  • Calculation: df.MonthlyIncome.mean().
  • Actual result: 6,502.93 per month (median 4,919).
  • HR interpretation: Half of employees earn below ~4,900; the higher mean is pulled up by a smaller group of senior earners. Pay policy discussions should reference the median and pay bands, not just the average.
  • Technical answer: Mean > median indicates right skew; the median is the more robust "typical" value.

KPI 6 — Average Years at Company¶

  • Business question: How long do employees typically stay?
  • Technical question: How skewed is tenure?
  • Calculation: df.YearsAtCompany.mean().
  • Actual result: 7.01 years (median 5).
  • HR interpretation: Most employees have 5 years or fewer; a long-tenured minority raises the average.
  • Technical answer: Tenure is right-skewed; banding it (0–1, 2–3, …) makes attrition patterns easier to read than a raw mean.

KPI 7 — Overtime Employee Percentage¶

  • Business question: How widespread is overtime?
  • Technical question: What is the prevalence of the binary OverTime flag?
  • Calculation: OT employees ÷ total × 100.
  • Actual result: 28.30 % of employees work overtime.
  • HR interpretation: More than a quarter of the workforce regularly works beyond standard hours — a structural workload pattern, not an exception.
  • Technical answer: A 28/72 split gives enough observations in both groups for reliable rate comparisons.

KPI 8 — Overtime Employee Attrition Rate¶

  • Business question: Do employees who work overtime leave more often?
  • Technical question: What is the conditional probability P(leave | overtime)?
  • Calculation: leavers among OT employees ÷ OT employees × 100.
  • Actual result: 30.53 %, versus 10.44 % for non-overtime employees. Overtime workers are 28.3 % of staff but 53.6 % of all leavers.
  • HR interpretation: Overtime workers leave at roughly three times the rate of others. This is the single most striking KPI and a priority area to investigate (association, not proof of cause).
  • Technical answer: Comparing conditional rates (rather than raw counts) removes the effect of group size.

KPI 9 — Average Job Satisfaction¶

  • Business question: How satisfied are employees with their jobs?
  • Technical question: Is it appropriate to average an ordinal 1–4 scale?
  • Calculation: df.JobSatisfaction.mean().
  • Actual result: 2.73 / 4; 38.7 % of employees rate it 1 or 2.
  • HR interpretation: Satisfaction leans positive overall, but almost four in ten employees report only low or medium satisfaction — a sizeable group to engage.
  • Technical answer: Averaging ordinal codes assumes equal spacing between levels; it is acceptable as a dashboard indicator, but distributions (U6) are more informative.

KPI 10 — Average Work-Life Balance¶

  • Business question: Do employees feel they have a healthy work-life balance?
  • Technical question: Same ordinal-averaging caveat as KPI 9.
  • Calculation: df.WorkLifeBalance.mean().
  • Actual result: 2.76 / 4; 5.4 % rate it 1 ("bad").
  • HR interpretation: Most employees rate work-life balance as 3 ("better"); the small "bad" group is analysed further in B10 and M5.
  • Technical answer: With most responses at level 3, the mean has limited variance — subgroup rates are more useful than the mean.
In [16]:

Phase 2 — 10 Univariate Analyses¶

Each variable is examined on its own to understand its distribution before relating it to attrition. Format: Business Question → Technical Question → Why It Matters → Code → Visualisation → Actual Finding → Interpretation.

U1 — Attrition¶

  • Business question: How many employees stay versus leave?
  • Technical question: How imbalanced is the target, and what does that imply for model evaluation?
  • Why it matters: The base rate sets expectations for every model metric and dictates the need for stratification.
In [17]:
vc = df["Attrition"].value_counts()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
axes[0].bar(vc.index, vc.values, color=[STAY_C, LEAVE_C])
for i, v in enumerate(vc.values):
    axes[0].text(i, v + 15, f"{v} ({v/vc.sum():.1%})", ha="center")
axes[0].set_title("U1 — Attrition count"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Employees")
axes[1].pie(vc.values, labels=vc.index, autopct="%1.1f%%", colors=[STAY_C, LEAVE_C], startangle=90,
            wedgeprops=dict(width=0.45))
axes[1].set_title("U1 — Attrition share")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "u01_attrition"); plt.show()
print(vc.to_frame("count").assign(share_pct=(vc / vc.sum() * 100).round(2)))

           count  share_pct
Attrition                  
No          1233     83.880
Yes          237     16.120
  • Actual finding: 1,233 stayed (83.88 %) and 237 left (16.12 %) — a 5.2 : 1 imbalance.
  • Interpretation: Leavers are the minority class HR cares about most. Any evaluation must focus on how well that minority is identified, not on overall accuracy.
  • Technical answer: This is a moderately imbalanced binary problem → stratified splitting, PR-AUC/recall/F1 as key metrics, and class-weighting or threshold tuning.

U2 — Age¶

  • Business question: What is the age profile of our workforce?
  • Technical question: What is the shape of the Age distribution (centre, spread, skew)?
  • Why it matters: Age profiles shape career-stage needs (early-career development vs. later-career retention).

U3 — MonthlyIncome¶

  • Business question: How is pay distributed across employees?
  • Technical question: Is income skewed, and which summary statistic is appropriate?
  • Why it matters: Pay competitiveness is a standard retention lever; skew affects how we compare groups.

  • Technical answer: Strong right skew → median/IQR are robust summaries; for modelling, trees are scale-invariant and Logistic Regression receives standardised inputs.

  • Business question: Which roles make up our workforce?
  • Technical question: How many categories are there, and are any too sparse for reliable rates?
  • Why it matters: Retention programmes are usually designed per role family.

  • Why it matters: Department heads own retention budgets and actions.

  • Technical answer: Department is largely nested within JobRole (partial redundancy). Both are kept; regularisation and tree splits handle the overlap.

U6 — JobSatisfaction¶

  • Business question: How satisfied are employees with their jobs?
  • Technical question: How is an ordinal Likert-type variable best summarised?
  • Why it matters: Satisfaction is a commonly cited, potentially actionable correlate of turnover.

Phase 3 — 10 Bivariate Analyses (Attrition vs. one factor)¶

We compare attrition rates (not raw counts) across groups, with the company average (16.1 %) as a reference line. For statistical support we report:

  • Categorical factors: chi-square test of independence and Cramér's V effect size (≈0.1 small, ≈0.3 medium, ≈0.5 large).
  • Numeric factors: Mann–Whitney U test (robust to skew) comparing leavers and stayers.

A small p-value says a difference is unlikely to be pure chance in this sample; it does not say the factor causes attrition.

In [27]:
bivariate_stats = []   # collected for a summary table at the end of Phase 3
def mw_test(col):
    a, b = df.loc[df.AttritionFlag == 1, col], df.loc[df.AttritionFlag == 0, col]
    p = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b).pvalue
    bivariate_stats.append([col, "Mann-Whitney U", p, np.nan])
    return pd.DataFrame({"Left (Yes)": [a.mean(), a.median()], "Stayed (No)": [b.mean(), b.median()]},
                        index=["mean", "median"]).round(2), p
def chi_test(col):
    v, p = cramers_v(df[col], df.AttritionFlag)
    bivariate_stats.append([col, "Chi-square", p, v])
    return v, p

  • Technical answer: Significant, non-linear relationship (a "floor" effect) — tree models can capture this shape directly.

B3 — Attrition vs Overtime¶

  • Business question: Do employees who work overtime leave more?
  • Technical question: Is OverTime statistically associated with attrition, and how strong is the effect?

Chi-square p = 8.16e-21 | Cramer's V = 0.244 | relative risk = 2.93x
  • Actual finding: 30.5 % attrition among overtime workers vs 10.4 % among others — a relative risk of 2.93× (χ² p ≈ 8.2 × 10⁻²¹, Cramér's V = 0.244, the strongest of the categorical factors tested).
  • Business interpretation: Overtime is the clearest single correlate of attrition in this data. HR should investigate why overtime is needed in the affected teams (understaffing, deadlines, role design).
  • Technical answer: Strong, highly significant association; small-to-medium effect size by Cramér's V conventions.

WorkLifeBalance Chi-square 9.73e-04 0.105 True
DistanceFromHome Mann-Whitney U 2.39e-03 nan True
Department Chi-square 4.53e-03 0.086 True

Phase 3 summary. All ten factors show statistically significant differences in attrition. By effect size, overtime and job role stand out (Cramér's V ≈ 0.24), followed by environment satisfaction, job satisfaction and work-life balance (≈ 0.10–0.12), with department weakest (0.09). Among numeric factors, income, tenure and age show the most significant differences.

Phase 4 — 10 Multivariate Analyses¶

Here we combine three or more variables to see whether patterns strengthen, weaken or reverse inside subgroups. Heatmap cells show attrition rate and headcount; cells with fewer than 20 employees are hatched, shown on a white label and marked with *. Those cells are shown for completeness but are not used to draw conclusions — with n < 20, a single leaver moves the rate by 5 percentage points or more.

M1 — Attrition × OverTime × JobRole¶

  • Business question: Is the overtime effect the same in every role, or concentrated in certain roles?
  • Technical question: Does OverTime interact with JobRole (i.e. does the overtime gap vary by role)?
  • Analytical reason: If overtime risk is role-specific, workload interventions can be targeted.
In [39]:

display(m1.sort_values("OT_gap_pp", ascending=False))

  • Actual finding: In almost every role, overtime workers leave more. The largest reliable gaps: Sales Representatives 66.7 % with overtime (n = 24) vs 28.8 % without, Laboratory Technicians 50.0 % (n = 62) vs 15.7 %, Research Scientists 34.0 % (n = 97) vs 7.2 %, and Sales Executives 33.0 % (n = 94) vs 11.2 %. Healthcare Representatives show no overtime uplift (5.4 % vs 7.4 %). Human Resources with overtime (38.5 %) rests on only 13 people.
  • HR interpretation: Overtime is most strongly associated with attrition in junior, front-line roles (Sales Reps, Lab Techs, Research Scientists). Senior roles (Managers, Directors) show low rates even with overtime. Workload reviews should start in those front-line roles.
  • Technical answer: Yes — the overtime gap varies widely by role, an interaction that tree models capture natively.

M2 — Attrition × Age × MonthlyIncome¶

  • Business question: Is it young people, low-paid people, or young and low-paid people who leave?
  • Technical question: Are age and income independent risk factors, or confounded with each other?
  • Analytical reason: Age and income are correlated (r ≈ 0.50), so their separate effects need disentangling.
In [40]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5))
rate_heatmap(axes[0], eda, "AgeBand", "IncomeQuartile", "M2 — Attrition rate by age band and income quartile")
for lab, c, a in [("Stayed", STAY_C, 0.35), ("Left", LEAVE_C, 0.75)]:
    s = df[df.Attrition == ("Yes" if lab == "Left" else "No")]
    axes[1].scatter(s.Age, s.MonthlyIncome, s=12, alpha=a, c=c, label=lab)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Age"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Monthly income"); axes[1].legend()
axes[1].set_title("M2 — Age vs income, coloured by attrition")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "m02_age_income"); plt.show()
  • Actual finding: Within the lowest income quartile, attrition falls with age: 43.2 % for 18–25 (n = 74), 34.9 % for 26–30 (n = 106), 22.9 % for 31–35, 15.2 % for 36–40. Within the youngest band, attrition also falls with income (43.2 % → 26.2 % → 16.7 %). The scatter shows leavers clustered in the lower-left (young, low-income) corner. Young high-earners barely exist (1 employee aged 18–25 in Q4), so that cell cannot be assessed.
  • HR interpretation: Both factors matter: being young and low-paid is associated with the highest attrition of any age-pay combination. This points to early-career pay progression as an area to review.
  • Technical answer: Age and income each retain an association within levels of the other, but sparse cells (young/high-income) mean their effects are partly confounded.

M3 — Attrition × Department × JobSatisfaction¶

  • Business question: Does low job satisfaction matter more in some departments?
  • Technical question: Is the satisfaction gradient consistent across departments?
  • Analytical reason: A consistent gradient suggests an organisation-wide issue; an inconsistent one suggests local management factors.

M4 — Attrition × YearsAtCompany × JobLevel¶

  • Business question: Is early-tenure attrition a junior-level issue?
  • Technical question: How does tenure risk vary across job levels?
  • Analytical reason: Separates onboarding issues from career-stage issues.

M5 — Attrition × OverTime × WorkLifeBalance¶

  • Business question: Is overtime only a problem when people feel their balance is bad?
  • Technical question: Does the overtime association persist after conditioning on self-reported balance?
  • Analytical reason: If overtime still matters among people reporting good balance, the survey item may not capture the full workload effect.

  • Technical question: Is the overall income–attrition gap a within-role or between-role effect (Simpson's-paradox check)?
  • Analytical reason: Determines whether pay review should focus on pay within roles or on low-paying roles as a whole.

Within roles, the gap is mixed: leavers earn less than stayers in Sales Representative, Research Scientist, Laboratory Technician and Human Resources (e.g. HR median 2,653 vs 3,669), but more in Healthcare Representative, Manager, Research Director, Sales Executive and Manufacturing Director (where leaver counts are small: e.g. Research Director has 2 leavers).

M7 — Attrition × Age × JobSatisfaction¶

  • Business question: Does job satisfaction matter equally for younger and older employees?
  • Technical question: Does the satisfaction gradient differ by age band?
  • Analytical reason: Determines whether engagement efforts should be age-tailored.
In [45]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
rate, n = rate_heatmap(ax, eda, "AgeBand", "JobSatisfaction", "M7 — Attrition rate by age band and job satisfaction")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "m07_age_jobsat"); plt.show()
  • Actual finding: For 18–25, attrition is high at all satisfaction levels (43.5 % at levels 1–2, ~31 % at levels 3–4; n = 23–41 per cell). The satisfaction gradient is clearest for 36–40 (21.6 % at level 1 vs 3.4 % at level 4) and 26–30 (30.5 % → 15.7 %). For 41+ there is no clear gradient.
  • HR interpretation: Among the youngest staff, high satisfaction does not bring attrition down to the company average — their departures may relate to career moves rather than dissatisfaction. Among mid-career staff, satisfaction is more clearly linked to staying.
  • Technical answer: Evidence of an age × satisfaction interaction, though the youngest-band cells are modest in size.

M8 — Attrition × DistanceFromHome × OverTime¶

  • Business question: Is the combination of long commutes and overtime especially risky?
  • Technical question: Do commute and overtime compound (interaction) or simply add?
  • Analytical reason: Long hours plus long travel could amplify fatigue — relevant for flexible-working policy.

  • Technical question: Do two engagement-related ordinal variables compound?

M10 — Attrition × TotalWorkingYears × YearsAtCompany¶

  • Business question: Are new joiners risky because they are new to us, or because they are new to work?
  • Technical question: How do overall career length and company tenure jointly relate to attrition?
  • Analytical reason: Separates early-career effects from onboarding effects.
In [48]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.8))
rate, n = rate_heatmap(ax, eda, "CareerBand", "TenureBand",
                       "M10 — Attrition rate by total working years and years at company")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "m10_career_tenure"); plt.show()
  • Actual finding: The highest reliable cell is 0–2 total working years and 0–1 years at the company: 49.0 % (n = 96). New joiners with 3–5 years' career experience show 40.9 % (n = 22), with 6–10 years 20.0 % (n = 40) and 11–20 years 20.9 % (n = 43). Long-tenured, long-career employees (21+ years, 11+ tenure) show 9.7 %. Empty cells are logically impossible (tenure cannot exceed career length).
  • HR interpretation: First-year attrition is highest for people at the very start of their careers; experienced hires in their first year leave at roughly the company average or modestly above. Graduate/early-career onboarding deserves particular attention.
  • Technical answer: Career length and tenure both contribute; their correlation (r ≈ 0.63) and the structural empty cells mean they should be interpreted together.

Feature Engineering & Preprocessing¶

Design decisions¶

Decision Choice Reason
Target AttritionFlag (1 = left) Positive class = the event HR wants to anticipate.
Predictors 30 cleaned columns (Stage 5) EDA band columns are excluded — they were created for readability and would duplicate raw features.
Nominal categoricals (7) OneHotEncoder(drop="if_binary", handle_unknown="ignore") No natural order (e.g. JobRole). Binary fields (OverTime, Gender) become a single 0/1 column. handle_unknown="ignore" keeps scoring safe if a new category appears.
Ordinal codes (e.g. JobSatisfaction, JobLevel, Education) Kept as ordered integers Their order is meaningful; one-hot would discard it.
Numeric scaling StandardScaler for Logistic Regression only LR coefficients and L2 regularisation are scale-sensitive; tree models are not, so they receive unscaled values (which also keeps SHAP plots in real units).
Leakage prevention Everything inside a scikit-learn Pipeline + ColumnTransformer Scaler means/SDs and encoder categories are learned from training folds only — during cross-validation and in the final fit.
Hand-crafted ratio features Not added Keeps the feature set transparent for HR stakeholders and SHAP; the tree models can learn interactions directly.
In [49]:
TARGET = "AttritionFlag"
X = df.drop(columns=["Attrition", TARGET])
y = df[TARGET]

categorical_features = X.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns.tolist()
numeric_features = X.select_dtypes(include="number").columns.tolist()
print(f"X shape: {X.shape} | y positive rate: {y.mean():.2%}")
print(f"\nNominal categorical ({len(categorical_features)}): {categorical_features}")
print(f"\nNumeric / ordinal ({len(numeric_features)}): {numeric_features}")

def make_ohe():
    return OneHotEncoder(drop="if_binary", handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)

preprocess_linear = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", StandardScaler(), numeric_features),
    ("cat", make_ohe(), categorical_features),
], verbose_feature_names_out=False)

preprocess_tree = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", "passthrough", numeric_features),
    ("cat", make_ohe(), categorical_features),
], verbose_feature_names_out=False)

X shape: (1470, 30) | y positive rate: 16.12%

Nominal categorical (7): ['BusinessTravel', 'Department', 'EducationField', 'Gender', 'JobRole', 'MaritalStatus', 'OverTime']

Numeric / ordinal (23): ['Age', 'DailyRate', 'DistanceFromHome', 'Education', 'EnvironmentSatisfaction', 'HourlyRate', 'JobInvolvement', 'JobLevel', 'JobSatisfaction', 'MonthlyIncome', 'MonthlyRate', 'NumCompaniesWorked', 'PercentSalaryHike', 'PerformanceRating', 'RelationshipSatisfaction', 'StockOptionLevel', 'TotalWorkingYears', 'TrainingTimesLastYear', 'WorkLifeBalance', 'YearsAtCompany', 'YearsInCurrentRole', 'YearsSinceLastPromotion', 'YearsWithCurrManager']

Train/Test Split¶

  • 80 % training / 20 % test, stratify=y, random_state=SEED.
  • Why stratify? With only 16 % leavers, a random split could, by chance, put noticeably more or fewer leavers in the test set, making test metrics unstable and unrepresentative. Stratification guarantees both sets keep the same ≈16 % leaver rate.
  • The test set is locked away. All tuning uses 5-fold stratified cross-validation inside the training set. The test set is used once per model for the final, unbiased evaluation — it is never used to choose hyper-parameters or the decision threshold.
In [50]:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.20, stratify=y, random_state=SEED)
ids_test = employee_ids.loc[X_test.index]
split_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Rows": [len(y_train), len(y_test)],
    "Leavers": [int(y_train.sum()), int(y_test.sum())],
    "Leaver rate %": [round(y_train.mean() * 100, 2), round(y_test.mean() * 100, 2)],
}, index=["Train", "Test"])
display(split_summary)

CV = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
SCORING = {"pr_auc": "average_precision", "roc_auc": "roc_auc", "recall": "recall",
           "precision": "precision", "f1": "f1"}
REFIT = "pr_auc"   # hyper-parameters are chosen on cross-validated PR-AUC
Rows Leavers Leaver rate %
Train 1176 190 16.160
Test 294 47 15.990

Evaluation framework¶

For every model we report, on the held-out test set at the default 0.50 threshold:

Metric HR meaning
Accuracy Share of all employees classified correctly — misleading under imbalance.
Precision Of the employees flagged as "at risk", how many actually left. Low precision = many unnecessary interventions.
Recall Of the employees who actually left, how many were flagged. Low recall = missed leavers.
F1 Harmonic mean of precision and recall.
ROC-AUC Probability the model ranks a random leaver above a random stayer (0.5 = random).
PR-AUC (average precision) Ranking quality focused on the minority class; random baseline ≈ 0.16 here. Primary tuning metric.

Hyper-parameter tuning maximises cross-validated PR-AUC because it is threshold-independent and focuses on the leaver class. Class-imbalance handling (class_weight, scale_pos_weight) is treated as a tunable choice rather than assumed.

In [51]:
results, test_probas, cv_summaries = {}, {}, {}

def evaluate(name, model, threshold=0.5):
    proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    pred = (proba >= threshold).astype(int)
    m = {"Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, pred), "Precision": precision_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0),
         "Recall": recall_score(y_test, pred), "F1": f1_score(y_test, pred),
         "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(y_test, proba)}
    results[name], test_probas[name] = m, proba
    return pd.Series(m).round(3), proba, pred

def cv_summary(name, search):
    r = search.cv_results_; i = search.best_index_
    s = {k: (r[f"mean_test_{k}"][i], r[f"std_test_{k}"][i]) for k in SCORING}
    cv_summaries[name] = s
    return pd.DataFrame(s, index=["CV mean", "CV std"]).round(3)

def plot_evaluation(name, proba, pred, fname):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix(y_test, pred), display_labels=["Stayed", "Left"]).plot(
        ax=axes[0], cmap="Blues", colorbar=False)
    axes[0].set_title(f"{name} — confusion matrix (t=0.50)"); axes[0].grid(False)
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, proba)
    axes[1].plot(fpr, tpr, color=ACCENT, lw=2, label=f"ROC-AUC = {roc_auc_score(y_test, proba):.3f}")
    axes[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="grey"); axes[1].set_xlabel("False positive rate")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("True positive rate (recall)"); axes[1].set_title("ROC curve"); axes[1].legend()
    pr, rc, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, proba)
    axes[2].plot(rc, pr, color=LEAVE_C, lw=2, label=f"PR-AUC = {average_precision_score(y_test, proba):.3f}")
    axes[2].axhline(y_test.mean(), ls="--", color="grey", label=f"Random = {y_test.mean():.3f}")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("Recall"); axes[2].set_ylabel("Precision"); axes[2].set_title("Precision-recall curve"); axes[2].legend()
    plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, fname); plt.show()

Model 1 — Logistic Regression (interpretable baseline)¶

L2-regularised logistic regression on standardised numeric features and one-hot categoricals. Tuned by 5-fold CV over the regularisation strength C and class_weight (None vs "balanced").

Logistic Regression — results in HR language¶

  • Tuning: CV selected C = 0.3 (moderate regularisation) and class_weight = None — un-weighted training ranked leavers slightly better (CV PR-AUC 0.651 ± 0.061; CV ROC-AUC 0.839). Imbalance is instead handled later by lowering the decision threshold.
  • Test set (294 employees, 47 leavers) at threshold 0.50: accuracy 0.867, precision 0.667, recall 0.340, F1 0.451, ROC-AUC 0.813, PR-AUC 0.591.
  • Confusion matrix: 16 leavers correctly flagged, 31 leavers missed, 8 stayers flagged unnecessarily, 239 stayers correctly not flagged.
  • What it means for HR: When this model flags someone at the default 0.50 cut-off, it is right two times out of three — but it only catches about one in three leavers. The ranking quality is good (PR-AUC 0.591 vs 0.16 for random guessing), which means a lower threshold can recover many more leavers (see Threshold Analysis).
  • Coefficients: after standardisation, the strongest positive associations are OverTime_Yes (+1.58), JobRole_Laboratory Technician (+0.80), BusinessTravel_Travel_Frequently (+0.75) and JobRole_Sales Representative (+0.55); the strongest negative associations include BusinessTravel_Non-Travel (−0.70), JobRole_Research Director (−0.49), EnvironmentSatisfaction (−0.43), TotalWorkingYears (−0.41) and Age (−0.39). These are conditional associations — each holds the other features constant — and are consistent with the EDA. They are not causal effects.

Model 2 — Random Forest¶

An ensemble of decision trees that captures non-linear effects and interactions (e.g. M1, M4, M8). Tuned with RandomizedSearchCV (30 candidates × 5 folds) over n_estimators, max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_features and class_weight.

Random Forest — results in HR language¶

  • Tuning: best configuration — 600 trees, unrestricted depth, min_samples_split = 10, min_samples_leaf = 2, max_features = "sqrt", class_weight = "balanced_subsample". CV PR-AUC 0.565 ± 0.070 (CV ROC-AUC 0.808) — clearly below the other two models.
  • Test set at 0.50: accuracy 0.827, precision 0.409, recall 0.191, F1 0.261, ROC-AUC 0.779, PR-AUC 0.409.
  • Confusion matrix: only 9 of 47 leavers caught; 38 missed; 13 false alarms.
  • What it means for HR: Despite class weighting, the forest's probabilities are compressed (only 22 test employees score ≥ 0.50), so at the default threshold it misses four in five leavers. Its 82.7 % accuracy is below the 84.0 % a "nobody leaves" rule would score on this test set — a concrete illustration of why accuracy is the wrong yardstick here.
  • Technical answer: With only ~190 training leavers and many weak, mostly additive signals, deep bagged trees add variance without capturing much extra structure. Random Forest is the weakest model on every ranking metric.

Model 3 — XGBoost¶

Gradient-boosted trees. Class imbalance is handled through scale_pos_weight, searched over 1 (no re-weighting), √(neg/pos) (partial) and neg/pos (full re-weighting), computed from the training labels only. Tuned with RandomizedSearchCV (40 candidates × 5 folds) over n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth, subsample, colsample_bytree, min_child_weight and scale_pos_weight. The test set plays no part in tuning.

XGBoost — results in HR language¶

  • Tuning: best configuration — 200 shallow trees (max_depth = 2), learning_rate = 0.1, subsample = 0.7, colsample_bytree = 0.5, min_child_weight = 3, scale_pos_weight = 1. Cross-validation preferred no re-weighting over √ratio (2.28) or full ratio (5.19) re-weighting for ranking quality; the threshold, not the loss weights, is used to trade precision for recall. CV PR-AUC 0.648 ± 0.051 (CV ROC-AUC 0.838).
  • Test set at 0.50: accuracy 0.861, precision 0.667, recall 0.255, F1 0.369, ROC-AUC 0.799, PR-AUC 0.523.
  • Confusion matrix: 12 of 47 leavers caught, 35 missed, 6 false alarms.
  • What it means for HR: Very similar to Logistic Regression in cross-validation; slightly weaker on this particular test set. The very shallow trees selected by CV (depth 2 = at most pairwise interactions) suggest the attrition signal in this dataset is largely additive — which also explains why a linear model competes so well.

Model Comparison & Selection¶

Selection rule (fixed before looking at the comparison)¶

  1. Primary criterion — cross-validated PR-AUC on the training set. It is threshold-independent, focuses on the leaver class, and does not touch the test set.
  2. Parsimony tie-break. If a simpler, more interpretable model is within one standard error of the best CV PR-AUC (SE = CV std / √5), the simpler model is preferred — differences that small are within fold-to-fold noise.
  3. Test-set metrics confirm, they do not decide. They are reported for transparency; using them to pick the winner would quietly turn the test set into a validation set.
  4. Accuracy is not used for selection (a do-nothing model scores 83.9 %).

Model comparison — interpretation and final selection¶

Model Accuracy Precision Recall F1 ROC-AUC PR-AUC CV PR-AUC (mean ± std)
Logistic Regression 0.867 0.667 0.340 0.451 0.813 0.591 0.651 ± 0.061
Random Forest 0.827 0.409 0.191 0.261 0.779 0.409 0.565 ± 0.070
XGBoost 0.861 0.667 0.255 0.369 0.799 0.523 0.648 ± 0.051

Test-set metrics at threshold 0.50; CV metrics from 5-fold cross-validation on the training set.

False positives vs. false negatives. For an attrition-risk tool:

  • A false negative (a leaver the model missed) means HR loses the chance to have a retention conversation — the organisation then bears the full replacement cost.
  • A false positive (a stayer flagged as at-risk) leads to an unnecessary but usually low-cost, supportive check-in — provided the flag is never used punitively.

This asymmetry makes recall especially relevant, but recall alone is not enough: a model that flags everyone has 100 % recall and is useless. Precision, F1 and especially PR-AUC (ranking quality on the minority class) and ROC-AUC must be considered together.

Selection.

  1. Logistic Regression has the highest cross-validated PR-AUC (0.651). XGBoost (0.648) is within one standard error (SE = 0.027) — statistically indistinguishable — and Random Forest (0.565) is clearly behind.
  2. Under the pre-stated parsimony rule, the simpler model wins the tie, and here the simpler model is also the outright CV leader.
  3. The held-out test set confirms rather than decides: Logistic Regression also has the best test ROC-AUC (0.813), PR-AUC (0.591), recall (0.340) and F1 (0.451).
  4. Interpretability is a decisive practical bonus: HR can see the direction and size of every association, audit the model for fairness and explain any score to stakeholders.

➡ Selected model: Logistic Regression (L2, C = 0.3). XGBoost is retained as a strong challenger and is used for tree-based SHAP analysis, where its agreement with Logistic Regression provides a robustness check.

Note: highest accuracy was not the criterion. All three models' accuracies (0.83–0.87) sit close to the 0.84 achieved by predicting "nobody leaves".

Classification Threshold Analysis¶

A model outputs a probability; HR must choose the cut-off above which an employee is flagged. 0.50 is a convention, not a business decision.

Method (no test-set tuning):

  1. Generate out-of-fold probabilities for every training employee with 5-fold CV (cross_val_predict) using the selected model's tuned configuration — each prediction comes from a model that did not see that employee.
  2. Sweep thresholds 0.05–0.90 and compute precision, recall, F1, F2, false positives and false negatives.
  3. Choose the threshold that maximises F2 — an F-score that weights recall twice as heavily as precision, reflecting that for a supportive intervention (a career conversation) a missed leaver is costlier than an unnecessary check-in.
  4. Apply that threshold once to the test set.
In [58]:
final_model = {"Logistic Regression": lr_model, "Random Forest": rf_model, "XGBoost": xgb_model}[SELECTED]
oof = cross_val_predict(final_model, X_train, y_train, cv=CV, method="predict_proba", n_jobs=-1)[:, 1]

def threshold_table(y_true, proba, thresholds):
    rows = []
    for t in thresholds:
        p = (proba >= t).astype(int)
        tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, p).ravel()
        rows.append({"Threshold": round(t, 2), "Flagged": tp + fp, "TP": tp, "FP": fp, "FN": fn, "TN": tn,
                     "Precision": precision_score(y_true, p, zero_division=0), "Recall": recall_score(y_true, p),
                     "F1": f1_score(y_true, p), "F2": fbeta_score(y_true, p, beta=2)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Threshold").round(3)

grid = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 0.91, 0.05), 2)
oof_table = threshold_table(y_train, oof, grid)
CHOSEN_T = float(oof_table["F2"].idxmax())
F1_T = float(oof_table["F1"].idxmax())
print(f"Out-of-fold (training) threshold sweep for {SELECTED}  |  OOF PR-AUC = {average_precision_score(y_train, oof):.3f}")
display(oof_table.style.highlight_max(subset=["F1", "F2"], color="#d4edda").format(precision=3))
print(f"F2-optimal threshold (selected): {CHOSEN_T:.2f}   |   F1-optimal threshold (reference): {F1_T:.2f}")
oof_table.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "threshold_analysis_train_oof.csv")

0.50 (default) 95 78 112 17 0.821 0.411 0.547 0.456
0.35 (F1-optimal) 177 113 77 64 0.638 0.595 0.616 0.603
0.20 (F2-optimal, selected) 328 139 51 189 0.424 0.732 0.537 0.639
  • Lowering the threshold from 0.50 to 0.20 raises recall from 41 % to 73 % — 61 more leavers identified — at the cost of 172 additional check-ins with employees who would have stayed.
  • Chosen threshold: 0.20 (maximises F2 on out-of-fold training predictions). If HR capacity for conversations is limited, 0.35 (F1-optimal) is a defensible, more conservative alternative; the table above lets HR choose based on capacity.

Applied once to the held-out test set (294 employees, 47 leavers):

  • At 0.50: 24 flagged — 16 leavers caught, 31 missed, 8 false alarms (recall 0.340, precision 0.667).
  • At 0.20: 72 flagged (24.5 % of employees) — 30 leavers caught, 17 missed, 42 false alarms (recall 0.638, precision 0.417, F1 0.504, F2 0.577).
  • A precision of 0.417 means roughly 2 in 5 flagged employees actually left — 2.6 × the 16 % base rate. Recall on the test set (0.64) is a little below the out-of-fold estimate (0.73), which is expected variation with only 47 test leavers.

Business implications. At 0.20 HR would hold ~1 supportive conversation for every 4 employees, and nearly two-thirds of eventual leavers would be among them. Because most flagged employees will not leave, the conversation must be framed as routine career and wellbeing support — never as an accusation or a performance concern.

SHAP Explainability¶

What SHAP does. For each employee, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) splits the model's output into additive contributions from each feature, relative to the average prediction. A positive SHAP value pushes that employee's predicted risk up; a negative value pushes it down.

What SHAP does not do. SHAP explains the model's predictions, not the real world. A large SHAP value for OverTime means the model relies on overtime to predict attrition — not that overtime causes people to leave. Correlated features (e.g. JobLevel and MonthlyIncome, r ≈ 0.95) can also share or swap credit.

Approach. As specified, SHAP is applied primarily to the best tree-based model (XGBoost) using the exact, fast TreeExplainer. Because the selection rule may favour Logistic Regression for deployment, we also compute linear SHAP for the Logistic Regression model and check whether the two models agree on the main risk factors — agreement between two very different model families makes the explanation more trustworthy. All SHAP values are computed on the test set (unseen employees), in log-odds units.

In [60]:
# --- XGBoost: tree SHAP on the test set ---
xgb_prep, xgb_clf = xgb_model.named_steps["prep"], xgb_model.named_steps["clf"]
feature_names = list(xgb_prep.get_feature_names_out())
X_test_tree = pd.DataFrame(xgb_prep.transform(X_test), columns=feature_names, index=X_test.index)
tree_explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(xgb_clf)
shap_xgb = tree_explainer(X_test_tree)
print(f"SHAP matrix: {shap_xgb.values.shape} | base value (log-odds) = {float(np.ravel(tree_explainer.expected_value)[0]):.3f}")

# Additivity check: base + sum(SHAP) == model log-odds
margin = xgb_clf.predict(X_test_tree.values, output_margin=True)
print("Max additivity error:", float(np.abs(shap_xgb.values.sum(1) + shap_xgb.base_values - margin).max()))

SHAP matrix: (294, 49) | base value (log-odds) = -1.660
Max additivity error: 2.384185791015625e-06

SHAP feature importance (mean |SHAP|) — XGBoost¶

In [61]:
plt.figure()
shap.plots.bar(shap_xgb, max_display=15, show=False)
plt.title("XGBoost — mean |SHAP value| (test set)"); fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(9, 6)
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "shap_importance_bar"); plt.show()

def direction(sv, Xdf):
    out = []
    for i, f in enumerate(Xdf.columns):
        x, s = Xdf[f].values.astype(float), sv[:, i]
        r = np.corrcoef(x, s)[0, 1] if np.std(x) > 0 else np.nan
        out.append([f, np.abs(s).mean(), r])
    t = pd.DataFrame(out, columns=["Feature", "Mean |SHAP|", "corr(value, SHAP)"]).set_index("Feature")
    t["Direction"] = np.where(t["corr(value, SHAP)"] > 0.1, "Higher value -> HIGHER risk",
                     np.where(t["corr(value, SHAP)"] < -0.1, "Higher value -> LOWER risk", "Mixed / non-linear"))
    return t.sort_values("Mean |SHAP|", ascending=False)

shap_dir_xgb = direction(shap_xgb.values, X_test_tree)
shap_dir_xgb.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "shap_feature_importance_xgb.csv")
display(shap_dir_xgb.head(15).round(3))

Global SHAP findings (XGBoost, test set)¶

The base value is −1.660 log-odds (≈ 16 % probability — the training base rate). Ranking by mean |SHAP|:

Features that push predicted attrition risk HIGHER

Feature Pattern the model uses
OverTime_Yes (#1, mean |SHAP| 0.605) Working overtime adds roughly +0.7 to +1.1 log-odds; not working overtime subtracts ~0.5.
StockOptionLevel = 0 (#2, 0.427) No stock options raises risk; any level ≥ 1 lowers it.
Younger Age (#3, 0.326) Ages below ~33 push risk up; mid-30s and older push it down.
High NumCompaniesWorked (#4, 0.325) 5+ previous employers pushes risk up sharply.
Longer DistanceFromHome (#5, 0.287) Distances above ~10 push risk up.
BusinessTravel_Travel_Frequently (#8, 0.248) Frequent travel pushes risk up.
More YearsSinceLastPromotion (#11, 0.214) Longer gaps since promotion push risk up (holding tenure constant).
JobRole_Laboratory Technician (#14, 0.166) Being a Lab Technician pushes risk up.

Features that push predicted attrition risk LOWER

Feature Pattern the model uses
High EnvironmentSatisfaction (#6, 0.278) Satisfaction ≥ 2 lowers risk; level 1 raises it substantially.
Higher MonthlyIncome (#7, 0.251) Higher pay lowers risk; the lowest incomes raise it.
More YearsWithCurrManager (#9, 0.234) Longer relationship with the current manager lowers risk.
High JobSatisfaction (#12, 0.192) Higher satisfaction lowers risk.
Department_Research & Development (#13, 0.180) Being in R&D lowers risk relative to Sales/HR.
High RelationshipSatisfaction (#15, 0.164) Higher satisfaction lowers risk.

Caveats. DailyRate (#10) ranks surprisingly high. In this dataset the rate fields do not reconcile with MonthlyIncome, so this may be the model fitting noise; it should not be interpreted as an HR lever. StockOptionLevel is entangled with MaritalStatus: every single employee has stock-option level 0 (verified in the Insights section), so the model cannot separate "no equity" from "single".

SHAP dependence plots — how the model uses key features¶

In [63]:
dep_feats = [f for f in shap_dir_xgb.index if X_test_tree[f].nunique() > 2][:4]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 9))
for ax, f in zip(axes.ravel(), dep_feats):

    ax.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8); ax.set_title(f"Dependence: {f}")
fig.suptitle("XGBoost SHAP dependence plots (colour = OverTime_Yes)", fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "shap_dependence"); plt.show()
print("Features shown:", dep_feats)

Features shown: ['StockOptionLevel', 'Age', 'NumCompaniesWorked', 'DistanceFromHome']

Dependence-plot findings¶

  • StockOptionLevel: a step function — level 0 receives SHAP values of roughly +0.3 to +0.55; levels 1–3 all receive negative values (≈ −0.3 to −0.6). The model treats "any equity vs none" as the key distinction.
  • Age: SHAP is positive (≈ +0.2 to +0.6) for employees in their 20s and early 30s and drops sharply to negative around ages 33–35, then stays mildly negative.
  • NumCompaniesWorked: 0 previous companies has strongly negative SHAP (≈ −0.7), 1–3 slightly negative, 4 near zero and 5 or more strongly positive (≈ +0.5 to +0.85). The unusual behaviour of the "0" category may reflect how this field was coded (e.g. whether the current employer is counted) and should be clarified with the data owner.
  • DistanceFromHome: negative below ~8, rising through ~10, and positive (up to ≈ +0.7) for the longest distances.
  • Colouring by OverTime_Yes shows no strong visual interaction in these four plots — the overtime effect is largely added on top, consistent with M5.

Individual explanations¶

  • Case A — Employee 959 (predicted 0.978; actually left). A 19-year-old Level-1 Sales Representative earning 2,121 per month, working overtime, one year in the company, no stock options. The largest upward pushes are OverTime_Yes (+1.03), young Age (+0.62), short YearsWithCurrManager (+0.59) and short TotalWorkingYears (+0.59). The only notable downward push is very high environment satisfaction (−0.27). The profile matches several high-risk groups found in the EDA simultaneously (front-line role + overtime + early career + low pay).
  • Case B — Employee 1804 (predicted 0.002; stayed). A 35-year-old Level-2 Manufacturing Director, no overtime, 7 years' tenure, stock-option level 1, job satisfaction 4. Risk is pulled down by no overtime (−0.52), DailyRate (−0.47), non-travel (−0.46) and stock options (−0.38).
  • Case C — Employee 1572 (predicted 0.003; actually left) — a missed leaver. A 53-year-old Level-3 Manufacturing Director with 33 years' tenure, no overtime and above-median pay. Every major factor points to "stay" (NumCompaniesWorked −0.74, no overtime −0.44, long manager tenure −0.42, long career −0.39). This profile could be consistent with retirement, but the dataset does not record the reason for leaving, so we cannot confirm it. It illustrates a structural limitation: the model predicts "leaving" without distinguishing voluntary resignation from retirement or other exits, and such departures are inherently hard to predict from these fields.

These explanations describe why the model scored each person as it did — they are not a diagnosis of why any individual actually left.

Do the two model families agree?¶

  • OverTime_Yes is the #1 driver in both models.
  • Five features appear in both top-10 lists: OverTime_Yes, Age, EnvironmentSatisfaction, NumCompaniesWorked and YearsWithCurrManager.
  • Direction agrees for every feature that appears in both models' top-15 lists (e.g. overtime, frequent travel, distance, years since last promotion and the Lab Technician role push risk up; environment, job and relationship satisfaction, age and stock options push it down).
  • Differences are explainable: XGBoost ranks StockOptionLevel (#2) and MonthlyIncome (#7) higher because trees capture the non-linear "level 0 vs ≥ 1" step and the low-income floor seen in B2; Logistic Regression spreads the same pay/level signal across JobRole dummies, TotalWorkingYears and JobLevel (all correlated with income). LR also gives more weight to JobSatisfaction, JobInvolvement and YearsSinceLastPromotion.

Conclusion: two very different algorithms rely on largely the same small set of workforce factors, in the same directions. This agreement — not any single SHAP plot — is what makes the explanation credible. It remains an explanation of model behaviour, not proof of causation.

Scoring output and model persistence¶

The selected model and its chosen threshold are saved together, and test-set risk scores are exported with EmployeeNumber for traceability. Risk bands are descriptive aids for prioritising supportive conversations — they are not performance judgements.

In [66]:
risk = pd.DataFrame({"EmployeeNumber": ids_test.values,
                     "ActualAttrition": np.where(y_test.values == 1, "Yes", "No"),
                     "PredictedProbability": test_probas[SELECTED].round(4)}, index=X_test.index)
risk["Flagged"] = risk.PredictedProbability >= CHOSEN_T
HIGH_T = max(0.70, CHOSEN_T + 0.05)   # "High" band starts at 0.70 (or just above the flag threshold)

                          labels=["Lower", "Elevated", "High"])

risk.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "test_set_risk_scores.csv", index=False)
display(rate_table(risk.assign(AttritionFlag=(risk.ActualAttrition == "Yes").astype(int)), "RiskBand"))

The bands separate risk well: the observed attrition rate rises from 7.7 % to 32.3 % across the first two bands. The "High" band's 100 % rate rests on only 10 employees and should be read as "very high", not as certainty. The saved artefact models/attrition_model.joblib contains the full preprocessing + model pipeline and the 0.20 threshold, so new employee records (with the same 30 input columns) can be scored with predict_proba directly.

Key Business Insights¶

Each insight is drawn only from results computed above. One extra cell first verifies the raw attrition rates for factors that SHAP highlighted but the 40 EDA analyses did not cover directly.
