Insight 1 — One in six employees left, and leavers are highly concentrated¶

  • Evidence: 237 of 1,470 employees left (16.1 %). Group rates range from 2.5 % (Research Directors) to 39.8 % (Sales Representatives) and 49.0 % (early-career first-year employees).
  • Interpretation: Attrition is not evenly spread; a handful of overlapping groups account for a disproportionate share.
  • Business significance: Targeted programmes for specific groups are likely to be more cost-effective than organisation-wide initiatives.

Insight 2 — Overtime is the strongest and most consistent attrition signal¶

  • Evidence: 30.5 % attrition with overtime vs 10.4 % without (2.93×; Cramér's V 0.244). Overtime workers are 28.3 % of staff but 53.6 % of leavers. OverTime_Yes is the #1 feature in both the Logistic Regression and XGBoost SHAP rankings.
  • Interpretation: Every analytical lens — rates, statistical tests, linear and tree models — points to overtime.
  • Business significance: Workload is a controllable factor. It is the first area HR should investigate with team leaders.

Insight 3 — Overtime risk concentrates in front-line roles and is not captured by WLB surveys¶

  • Evidence: With overtime, attrition reaches 66.7 % for Sales Representatives (n = 24), 50.0 % for Laboratory Technicians (n = 62), 34.0 % for Research Scientists (n = 97) and 33.0 % for Sales Executives (n = 94) (M1). Among employees rating work-life balance "Better" (3), overtime workers still leave at 28.7 % vs 8.5 % (M5).
  • Interpretation: Overtime is associated with attrition mainly in junior roles, and survey scores alone under-detect the strain.
  • Business significance: Monitor actual overtime hours by role, not only survey sentiment.

Insight 4 — The first year, especially for early-career Level-1 hires, is the danger zone¶

  • Evidence: 34.9 % attrition in the first 0–1 years (B8); 44.1 % for Level-1 employees in their first year (M4, n = 136); 49.0 % for employees with ≤ 2 years' total experience in their first year (M10, n = 96). Employees with 0 years under their current manager show 32.3 % attrition.
  • Interpretation: Early-career onboarding and early relationships with managers appear to be critical periods.
  • Business significance: Structured onboarding and early manager check-ins for graduate and entry-level hires are a high-leverage focus.

Insight 5 — Young and low-paid is the highest-risk age-pay combination¶

  • Evidence: 35.8 % attrition for ages 18–25; 29.3 % in the lowest income quartile (≤ 2,911); 43.2 % for those who are both (M2, n = 74). Age is #3 in XGBoost SHAP.
  • Interpretation: Age and pay each retain an association within levels of the other.
  • Business significance: Early-career pay progression is a plausible retention lever to examine.

Insight 6 — Role matters far more than department¶

  • Evidence: Job role Cramér's V = 0.242 vs department 0.086. Sales Representatives 39.8 %, Laboratory Technicians 23.9 %, HR 23.1 % vs Research Directors 2.5 % and Managers 4.9 %.
  • Interpretation: Department-wide averages hide large role-level differences.
  • Business significance: Retention budgets and actions should be allocated by role family rather than by department.

Insight 7 — The company-wide pay gap is mostly a role-mix effect¶

  • Evidence: Leavers' median income is 3,202 vs 5,204 for stayers (B2), but within roles the gap is mixed (M6): leavers earn less than stayers in Sales Representative, Research Scientist, Laboratory Technician and HR roles, but not in senior roles. In Logistic Regression, MonthlyIncome ranks only #23 by SHAP once role and level are included.
  • Interpretation: Leavers are concentrated in low-paying roles; pay within those roles may still matter.
  • Business significance: A within-role pay-positioning review for the four low-paid, high-attrition roles is better supported than a blanket pay increase.

Insight 8 — Engagement and environment satisfaction are consistent, measurable signals¶

  • Evidence: Attrition at the lowest level vs highest level — Environment satisfaction 25.4 % vs 13.5 %; Job satisfaction 22.8 % vs 11.3 %; Job involvement 33.7 % vs 9.0 %. EnvironmentSatisfaction is in the top 10 of both models' SHAP rankings.
  • Interpretation: Self-reported engagement measures carry real predictive signal, mostly at the dissatisfied end of the scale.
  • Business significance: Regular pulse surveys provide early, actionable warning signs at team level.

Insight 9 — "No stock options" and "single" cannot be separated in this data¶

  • Evidence: Stock-option level 0 shows 24.4 % attrition vs 9.4 % (level 1) and 7.6 % (level 2); single employees show 25.5 % vs 12.5 % married. The crosstab shows all 470 single employees have stock-option level 0. StockOptionLevel is #2 in XGBoost SHAP.
  • Interpretation: The model's reliance on stock options may partly reflect marital status (or vice versa); the data cannot tell which.
  • Business significance: Before acting on equity as a retention lever, HR should check whether this pattern reflects a real eligibility policy or a dataset artefact.

Insight 10 — Frequent travel and long commutes add risk, particularly with overtime¶

  • Evidence: Frequent travellers 24.9 % vs non-travellers 8.0 %; distance 21–29 units 22.1 % vs 13.8 % for 1–5 (B9); long-commute overtime workers 42.6 % (M8, n = 61). Both appear in both models' top-15 SHAP features.
  • Interpretation: Time-burden factors appear to compound workload.
  • Business significance: Travel rotation and flexible/hybrid arrangements are practical areas to explore for affected roles.

Insight 11 — Attrition is predictable enough to prioritise support, not to make individual judgements¶

  • Evidence: Logistic Regression achieves CV PR-AUC 0.651 (vs 0.16 random baseline) and test ROC-AUC 0.813. At threshold 0.20 it identified 30 of 47 test-set leavers (63.8 %) while flagging 72 of 294 employees; 41.7 % of flagged employees left (2.6× base rate). The "Lower" risk band had only 7.7 % attrition.
  • Interpretation: The model ranks risk well but makes many individual errors.
  • Business significance: Suitable for prioritising supportive outreach and monitoring groups; unsuitable for any decision about an individual's employment.

HR Recommendations¶

Each recommendation is tied to the evidence above. All are framed as areas to investigate or pilot — the analysis is observational, so the effect of any intervention should be measured (ideally with a comparison group) before scaling.

# Recommendation Evidence Suggested first step
1 Overtime review in front-line roles Insights 2, 3 (OT 30.5 % vs 10.4 %; Sales Rep/Lab Tech/Research Scientist/Sales Exec with OT 33–67 %) Audit overtime hours and staffing levels in these four roles; pilot overtime caps or additional headcount in one team and track attrition vs a comparable team.
2 Structured first-year onboarding for early-career hires Insight 4 (first-year 34.9 %; Level-1 first-year 44.1 %; early-career first-year 49.0 %) 30/60/90-day check-ins, buddy/mentor assignment and clear role expectations for Level-1 and graduate hires.
3 Within-role pay-positioning review for low-paid, high-attrition roles Insights 5, 7 (lowest quartile 29.3 %; young + low-paid 43.2 %; within-role gaps in 4 roles) Benchmark Sales Representative, Laboratory Technician, Research Scientist and HR pay against market; review early-career pay progression.
4 Clear progression paths out of Level 1 Insight 4 & M4 (Level 1 with 6–10 years' tenure still 21.6 %; Level 1 overall 26.3 % vs 9.7 % Level 2); YearsSinceLastPromotion pushes risk up in both models Publish promotion criteria (e.g. Sales Rep → Sales Exec, Lab Tech → Research Scientist) and review Level-1 employees with long time-in-grade.
5 Manager continuity and stay conversations Insight 4 (0 years with current manager 32.3 %); YearsWithCurrManager lowers risk in both models Minimise manager changes for new hires; train managers to run regular "stay interviews".
6 Team-level engagement pulse surveys Insight 8 (low environment satisfaction 25.4 %; low involvement 33.7 %) Quarterly anonymous pulse on environment, job satisfaction and involvement; act on team-level aggregates (not individual scores).
7 Travel and commute flexibility Insight 10 (frequent travel 24.9 %; long commute + OT 42.6 %) Review frequent-travel rotations; pilot hybrid days or flexible hours for long-commute overtime workers where roles allow.
8 Verify the equity eligibility pattern before using it as a lever Insight 9 (all single employees at stock level 0) Check whether stock-option eligibility genuinely depends on marital status (which would raise fairness and legal questions) or is a data artefact.
9 Deploy the model only as a governed, supportive prioritisation tool Insight 11 (recall 0.64 at t = 0.20; many false positives) Score monthly; route "Elevated/High" employees to optional career/wellbeing conversations; never use scores for promotion, pay, performance or termination decisions; keep a human in the loop.
10 Fairness review and better data before production Limitations; Gender, MaritalStatus, Age are model inputs Run a fairness audit and test removing protected attributes; start recording exit reason (voluntary/retirement/other), timestamped snapshots and engagement trends; retrain and validate on the organisation's own data.

Limitations¶

  • Dataset size. 1,470 employees and only 237 leavers (47 in the test set). Metric estimates are noisy (e.g. CV PR-AUC standard deviations of 0.05–0.07), and many subgroup cells are too small to interpret.
  • Class imbalance. At 16 % positives, small changes in a few predictions move precision and recall noticeably; we mitigated this with stratification, PR-AUC-based tuning and threshold analysis, but uncertainty remains.
  • Synthetic / demo nature. The IBM HR Analytics dataset is a fictional dataset created by IBM data scientists for demonstration. Some fields behave unrealistically (e.g. DailyRate, HourlyRate and MonthlyRate do not reconcile with MonthlyIncome; PerformanceRating only takes values 3–4; every single employee has stock-option level 0). Findings illustrate a method; they are not facts about a real organisation.
  • Representativeness and generalisation. One synthetic company in one snapshot. Patterns, the model and the chosen threshold must be re-estimated and validated on each organisation's own data before use.
  • Observational, not causal. All findings — rates, tests, coefficients and SHAP values — are associations. Overtime, for example, may be a symptom of understaffing or of a role's nature rather than a cause of leaving. Only controlled pilots can establish intervention effects.
  • Omitted variables. No data on manager quality, external job market, team dynamics, commute mode, remote-work status, compensation relative to market, exit reason or life events. Omitted factors may confound the observed associations.
  • Exit type not recorded. Attrition does not distinguish voluntary resignation, retirement, dismissal or end of contract (see SHAP Case C). A model of voluntary turnover would require this distinction.
  • Snapshot timing / potential leakage. The extraction date is undocumented; tenure-related fields of leavers may have been captured at exit. In production, features must be taken as of the scoring date.
  • Model uncertainty. Logistic Regression and XGBoost are statistically tied in CV. At the chosen threshold, ~58 % of flagged test employees did not leave and ~36 % of leavers were missed. Probabilities have not been externally calibrated.
  • Correlated features. JobLevel/MonthlyIncome (r ≈ 0.95) and the tenure variables share signal, so individual coefficients and SHAP attributions can shift between correlated partners.
  • Ethics and fairness. Sensitive attributes (Gender, MaritalStatus, Age) are inputs. A formal fairness assessment, legal review and transparent communication to employees are prerequisites for any operational use.

Final Conclusion¶

Business problem. Employee attrition is costly and disruptive. The HR Manager needed to know how many people leave, where attrition concentrates, which characteristics are associated with it, and whether it can be predicted reliably enough to target supportive retention efforts.

Dataset. The IBM HR Analytics dataset (1,470 employees, 35 columns) was complete and clean: no missing values, duplicates or invalid entries. Four columns (three constants and an identifier) were removed with justification; genuine high-value "outliers" were retained.

EDA. Ten KPIs established a 16.1 % attrition rate (237 leavers) and showed that the 28.3 % of employees who work overtime leave at 30.5 % versus 10.4 % for others. Univariate analyses profiled a mid-career, right-skewed-income workforce. Bivariate analyses (with chi-square / Mann-Whitney tests) found overtime and job role to have the strongest associations, followed by satisfaction measures, tenure, age and income. Multivariate analyses showed how these risks compound: front-line roles with overtime (up to 66.7 %), Level-1 first-year employees (44.1 %), early-career first-year employees (49.0 %), young low-paid employees (43.2 %) and long-commute overtime workers (42.6 %), while flagging every subgroup too small to trust.

Major attrition patterns. Workload (overtime), career stage (age, tenure, job level, early-career experience), role and pay positioning, engagement (environment/job satisfaction, involvement), equity (stock options, entangled with marital status) and time burden (travel, commute).

Machine learning. A leakage-safe scikit-learn Pipeline with ColumnTransformer (one-hot encoding; scaling for Logistic Regression) was trained on a stratified 80/20 split. Three models were tuned by 5-fold cross-validated PR-AUC without touching the test set.

Model comparison and selection. Logistic Regression (CV PR-AUC 0.651; test ROC-AUC 0.813, PR-AUC 0.591) and XGBoost (CV PR-AUC 0.648) were statistically tied; Random Forest trailed (0.565). Accuracy was rejected as a selection criterion. Logistic Regression was selected on cross-validated PR-AUC, parsimony and interpretability, and was confirmed by the best test-set ranking metrics.

Threshold. Using out-of-fold training predictions, an F2-optimal threshold of 0.20 was chosen to prioritise recall. On the held-out test set it identified 30 of 47 leavers (recall 0.64) while flagging 72 of 294 employees (precision 0.42, 2.6× the base rate).

SHAP explainability. TreeSHAP on XGBoost and linear SHAP on Logistic Regression agreed that overtime is the strongest driver of predicted risk, and that both models push predictions up for frequent travel, long commutes, many previous employers, time since promotion and the Lab Technician role, and down for higher environment and job satisfaction, age, stock options and manager tenure. SHAP explains the models' predictions, not the causes of attrition.

HR implications and recommendations. The evidence supports investigating overtime in front-line roles, early-career onboarding, within-role pay positioning and progression from Level 1, manager continuity, engagement pulse surveys and travel/commute flexibility — and deploying the model only as a governed, supportive prioritisation tool with fairness review.

Limitations. The dataset is small, imbalanced and synthetic; findings are observational; exit reasons and many relevant factors are absent. The approach is transferable, but the specific numbers, model and threshold must be rebuilt and validated on real organisational data before any decisions are made.
